strengths: The approach is well motivated: learning a low-dimensional conditioning variable for future-configuration generation offers a plausible extension of time-lagged autoencoders to richer conditional distributions.

The strongest empirical result is the substantially lower maximum potential energy of successful steered trajectories: TLC reports 33.58 kJ/mol versus approximately 755–904 kJ/mol for learned baselines, while achieving the highest reported target-hit percentage.

Evaluation includes two downstream sampling methods, five relevant learned baselines, a dihedral-angle reference, and ablations of input representation and autocorrelation regularization. OPES results demonstrate that TLC can recover a reasonable free-energy difference.
weaknesses: The evidence is too narrow for the claimed general contribution. All experiments concern one small, canonical system, alanine dipeptide, with a single learned CV and one lag time. There is no demonstration on more complex molecular systems, higher-dimensional slow processes, or computational scaling.

The experiments do not isolate the value of time-lagged generative learning. Missing controls include zero-lag generation, shuffled future frames within states, and an autocorrelation-only encoder with matched inputs. The substantial representation effect in Table 3 also motivates testing DeepTICA and the discriminative baselines with the same aligned-coordinate inputs.

The claim of learning slow dynamics is insufficiently established. Removing all training pairs whose endpoints have different phi signs changes the conditional distribution being learned and removes direct evidence of interstate dynamics. Low-energy forced paths and accurate equilibrium free-energy differences do not by themselves establish recovery of slow dynamical modes; kinetic, spectral, or committor-based validation is absent.

The SMD comparison needs stronger controls and uncertainty analysis. Results use method-specific force constants selected to maximize success under a permissive 1000 kJ/mol energy threshold, but no success-versus-energy curves or steering-duration sensitivity are provided. Energy is averaged only over successful trajectories, whose proportions differ substantially. TLC's target-hit improvement over TAE is only 60.93% versus 58.59%, without uncertainty across independently trained models.

OPES provides evidence of competitiveness rather than improvement: all methods have mean free-energy differences within the stated tolerance, and several baselines have substantially smaller reported variability than TLC. Counting minima in differently parameterized one-dimensional free-energy profiles is also not sufficient evidence that additional physical metastable states or slower modes have been recovered.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The manuscript omits the autocorrelation weight, detailed generative architecture, optimizer and training schedule, training sample count, and model-selection protocol. Equation (7) conflates molecular time and flow time and does not clearly specify the interpolated flow input. Appendix C contains an unfinished code-availability statement rather than a usable resource.

Several reporting inconsistencies need resolution: the stated force-constant search ends at 1000, but Table 1 uses 1200 for TAE; the text identifies DeepTICA as having the smallest RMSD although VDE does; and the stated 0.5-degree target-hit criterion needs clarification against the plotted target region. Table 3 also shows a large success-rate change when removing autocorrelation, from 60.93% to 97.27%, which deserves fuller analysis than the description of a minor tradeoff.

strengths: The method addresses an important problem: learning collective variables that support effective molecular sampling. Conditioning a flow-matching model on a learned time-lagged bottleneck is a plausible extension of predictive representation learning.
Table 1 reports a substantial reduction in successful-path maximum energy relative to the learned baselines, alongside the highest target-hit percentage among those baselines.
Evaluation includes two downstream sampling protocols, five relevant learned baselines, four OPES simulation seeds, and ablations of input representation and autocorrelation regularization.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to alanine dipeptide, a small, extensively studied system with known collective variables. There is no evidence of scalability, robustness across molecular systems, or practical benefit commensurate with the additional generative-model complexity.

The central claim of learning slow transition dynamics is insufficiently established. Removing all training pairs with opposite signs of phi alters the transition distribution and allows basin membership alone to achieve high autocorrelation. Successful biased transitions do not establish recovery of the true slow modes; kinetic or committor validation and comparisons with unfiltered training would strengthen this claim.

The contribution combines existing time-lagged encoding, conditional flow matching, and VDE-style autocorrelation. Ablations do not isolate the benefit of temporal generative modeling from static conditional generation or autocorrelation alone, and there is no lag-time sensitivity study. Representation differences also complicate comparisons with DeepLDA, DeepTDA, and DeepTICA.

The SMD comparison leaves important confounds unresolved. Force constants are selected to maximize success under a permissive 1000 kJ/mol energy ceiling, while energy is averaged only over successful trajectories. Success–energy tradeoff curves and uncertainty across independently trained models are needed. TLC's 60.93% hit rate is only slightly above TAE's 58.59%, and remains substantially below the dihedral reference's 100%.

OPES establishes competitive performance rather than an advantage: TLC gives 9.83 ± 1.15 kJ/mol against the reference's 10.06 ± 0.22, while several baselines are closer and less variable. Approximately uniform phi coverage and the number of minima in a learned-coordinate free-energy profile are insufficient evidence of correct slow dynamics; profile shape also depends on coordinate parameterization.

Reproducibility and technical specification are incomplete. Equation (7) conflates molecular time with flow time and does not clearly specify the interpolated noisy input or all sampling variables. The manuscript omits key optimization settings, the autocorrelation weight, and detailed generative-backbone configuration; the code-availability statement is unfinished. Appendix C specifies a force-constant search ending at 1000, but Table 1 uses 1200 for TAE. Appendix A also describes autocorrelation as degrading SMD performance despite improving both reported RMSD and maximum energy.

strengths: The approach is well motivated: learning a low-dimensional condition for time-lagged generative prediction is a plausible extension of time-lagged autoencoders to stochastic future configurations.

The strongest result is the substantially lower maximum energy along successful steered-MD trajectories: TLC reports 33.58 ± 15.19 kJ/mol versus approximately 755–904 kJ/mol for learned baselines, while achieving the highest reported target-hit rate among them.

Evaluation uses two downstream enhanced-sampling methods, five relevant learned baselines, and dihedral-angle references. OPES results include four simulation replicates, and ablations examine input representation and autocorrelation regularization.
TLC recovers an OPES free-energy difference consistent with the reference, supporting its practical usefulness on alanine dipeptide.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to alanine dipeptide, a small, extensively studied benchmark, using a single CV dimension and lag time. There is no evidence of scalability or effectiveness on more complex molecular systems, and no computational-cost comparison. This is insufficient support for a broadly significant methodological contribution.

The central claim of learning slow dynamics is supported indirectly. Removing cross-basin training pairs changes the transition distribution being learned and allows basin identity alone to achieve strong autocorrelation. No kinetic-spectrum, implied-timescale, committor, or conditional-generation validation establishes that TLC captures the relevant dynamics beyond this benchmark's downstream behavior.

The contribution of generative modeling is not adequately isolated. The method combines an established generative backbone with a predictive bottleneck and existing autocorrelation regularization. There is no zero-lag control or matched encoder trained with autocorrelation alone. Moreover, the representation ablation causes a large performance collapse, but DeepLDA, DeepTDA, and DeepTICA are not tested with the same aligned-coordinate representation.

The SMD comparison needs stronger controls. Each method uses a different force constant selected to maximize success under a permissive 1000 kJ/mol energy threshold, and energies are averaged only over successful trajectories. Success-versus-energy curves and comparisons at matched energy budgets are needed to assess robustness. TLC's hit rate of 60.93% is only slightly above TAE's 58.59%, without uncertainty on that difference; low steered-path energy alone does not establish correct transition-path statistics.

OPES demonstrates competitiveness rather than improvement: TLC's free-energy estimate has substantially greater reported variability than DeepTICA, DeepTDA, and VDE. Counting minima in differently parameterized one-dimensional free-energy profiles, or seeking a uniform phi distribution under bias, does not by itself demonstrate recovery of slow dynamical modes.

Important implementation details and mathematical definitions remain incomplete. Equation (7) conflates physical time/configurations with flow interpolation time/configurations rather than specifying the conditional flow-matching sampling procedure. The manuscript omits the autocorrelation weight, optimizer, training schedule, dataset split, and detailed generative architecture; the code-availability sentence is unfinished. The stated SMD force-constant search ends at 1000, whereas Table 1 uses 1200 for TAE, and the stated 0.5-degree hit threshold requires clarification. These issues materially hinder reproduction.

strengths: The proposed use of a frozen BioEmu model as a conditional generative objective for learning compact collective variables is a plausible and useful connection between molecular foundation models and enhanced sampling.

The evaluation includes substantial explicit-solvent simulations on three proteins, multiple established learned-CV baselines, structural interpretation, and supplementary ablations of time-lagged conditioning, backbone freezing, encoder size, and conditioning placement.

The combined learned-CV/RMSD steering results are promising: target-hit rates reach 100% on Chignolin and 93.8% on BBA, substantially exceeding the reported learned-CV baselines. BIOEMU-CV also achieves the lowest reported mean free-energy errors across the three proteins.
weaknesses: The central transition-path evidence depends on an additional target-informed coordinate. Appendix B.4 reveals that steering uses fθ(x) minus target RMSD, rather than the learned CV alone. Appendix D.3 reports essentially unsuccessful steering with BIOEMU-CV alone: 0–6.2% target hits on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA. Without an RMSD-only baseline, the incremental benefit of the learned CV is unresolved. This qualification should be prominent in the main results.

Free-energy comparisons use method-dependent definitions of folded and unfolded states obtained by bisecting each CV's range. Consequently, different methods estimate different physical quantities: for Trp-cage, reference free energies range from -1.45 to 4.15 kJ/mol, and BBA references also change sign. Common structural basin definitions are needed to compare folding free-energy accuracy fairly; PMF errors along different learned coordinates are likewise not directly equivalent.

The OPES statistical evidence is weak. One of four runs is removed for Trp-cage and BBA based on its final free-energy deviation, although trapping is itself an important failure of enhanced sampling. Errors are reported as differences between averaged estimates and references, allowing cancellation across runs. Large remaining variability and the 7.22 kJ/mol BBA error limit claims of reliable convergence. All-run results, per-run absolute errors, and uncertainty on improvements are needed.

The evidence that time-lagged generation specifically captures slow dynamics remains mixed. Table 13's no-lag variant has better PMF MAE than the proposed method (1.41 versus 3.07), despite the text claiming improvement on both tasks. BIOEMU-CV does not consistently lead the VAMP or committor comparisons. Held-out kinetic validation and a physical lag-time sensitivity study would strengthen the mechanistic claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The protein-training lag in physical units, construction of time-lagged pairs after random frame sampling, adapter architecture, optimizer, learning rate, and training cost are not adequately specified. Appendix B.2 gives a fixed 45-input architecture despite proteins having different numbers of pairwise distances, and its architecture description is difficult to reconcile with the later 48K-parameter encoder.

The importance of foundation-model pretraining is not isolated: freezing versus unfreezing does not establish an advantage over an appropriately matched unpretrained generative model. Possible overlap between BioEmu pretraining and the evaluation proteins or trajectories is not discussed. Three small proteins trained using long equilibrium trajectories provide limited evidence for broader scalability or usefulness when rare-event data are scarce.

Rapid, strongly biased steering and maximum total potential energy among successful trajectories do not establish physically representative transition-path sampling. Success-conditioned energy comparisons involve different trajectory subsets and may include substantial solvent contributions. Additional path-quality validation and clearer energy definitions are needed.

strengths: The method offers a plausible and useful application of pretrained molecular generative models: learning a compact CV through time-lagged conditioning while keeping BioEmu frozen.

The evaluation includes substantial explicit-solvent simulations on three proteins, three established learned-CV baselines, structural analyses, and several ablations. This goes beyond evaluation on alanine dipeptide alone.

The combined CV-plus-RMSD steering protocol achieves notable improvements on Chignolin and BBA: target-hit rates increase to 100% and 93.8%, respectively, versus 37.5% and 18.8% for DeepTICA. The appendix also reports negative results, including failures without RMSD guidance.
weaknesses: The principal transition-path results do not isolate the learned CV's contribution. Appendix B.4 reveals that steering uses fθ(x) minus target Cα-RMSD, rather than the learned CV alone. Table 15 shows BIOEMU-CV alone achieves only 0–6.2% target hits on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA under the tested settings. Although every method receives RMSD guidance, the missing RMSD-only baseline prevents establishing the learned component's incremental benefit. This qualification should be central to the main presentation.

The free-energy benchmark compares different physical state partitions across methods. Folded and unfolded basins are defined by halving each method's CV range, producing substantially different reference folding free energies for the same protein—for example, −17.24 for VDE versus approximately −3.7 for other Chignolin CVs. Consequently, errors do not measure a common folding observable. A shared structural state definition is needed; PMF MAEs on different learned coordinates also require caution when used to rank methods.

Statistical support for thermodynamic superiority is weak. Table 1 reports large variability, and BIOEMU-CV's BBA estimate remains 9.99 ± 5.43 against a reference of 2.77. The reported absolute error is calculated from the mean estimate, which can conceal cancellation between inaccurate runs. Furthermore, removing whichever of four runs deviates most from their mean excludes trapping failures that are directly relevant to CV quality. All-run results, per-run errors, and uncertainty on comparisons are needed.

The evidence does not establish that time-lagged generation specifically recovers better slow coordinates. The no-time-lag ablation actually improves Chignolin PMF MAE from 3.07 to 1.41, despite the text claiming better performance on both downstream tasks with time-lagging. Committor correlation is essentially tied with TAE and below VDE, while VAMP results are mixed. There is no lag-sensitivity study or direct validation of the learned conditional dynamics.

The value of foundation-model pretraining is insufficiently isolated. Freezing versus unfreezing pretrained BioEmu does not distinguish the benefit of pretraining from that of a diffusion reconstruction objective. A matched generative model trained from scratch and clarification of overlap between BioEmu pretraining data and evaluation proteins would strengthen attribution. PCA/TICA comparisons are limited to Trp-cage, and conventional structural CVs are not comprehensively benchmarked.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for the central method. The protein-training lag and its physical units, construction of time-lagged pairs after random frame selection, conditioning-network specification, and optimization settings are not adequately documented. Appendix B.2 gives a universal 45-input architecture despite different protein feature dimensions, and independent training-seed variability is not reported.

The transition-path metrics support successful forced folding more directly than physically faithful transition-path sampling. Maximum potential energy along strongly driven trajectories, evaluated only for successful paths, does not establish correct path probabilities or kinetics. Combined with the small protein set and the unresolved evaluation issues, the evidence is insufficient for the paper's broader claims about reliable slow-mode learning and scalability.

strengths: The method offers a promising use of a frozen protein foundation model: learning a compact CV through time-lagged conditional generation while keeping the deployed encoder small.
The evaluation includes substantial explicit-solvent simulations on three proteins, two downstream tasks, and comparisons with DeepTICA, TAE, and VDE using shared input descriptors and training data.
The combined CV–RMSD steering results are encouraging: BIOEMU-CV achieves 100% target hits on Chignolin and 93.8% on BBA, substantially exceeding the tested baselines.

The appendix provides useful ablations of time-lagged conditioning, backbone freezing, encoder size, conditioning placement, and RMSD assistance. Structural sensitivity and secondary-structure analyses add interpretability.
weaknesses: The strongest downstream result does not isolate the learned CV's contribution. Appendix B.4 reveals that the main steering experiments use fθ(x) minus target RMSD, rather than the learned CV alone. Without RMSD assistance, Table 15 reports only 0–6.2% target hits for BIOEMU-CV on Chignolin and 0% on Trp-cage and BBA under the tested settings. An RMSD-only baseline and controlled mixing-weight comparisons are essential to establish the added value of BIOEMU-CV.

The free-energy comparisons use method-dependent physical state definitions: folded and unfolded basins are obtained by halving each CV's range. Consequently, Table 1 gives substantially different reference folding free energies for the same protein, sometimes with opposite signs. These results measure agreement with different partitions rather than a common folding observable. Evaluation should additionally use shared structural basin definitions and retain numerical results for unsuccessful methods.

The statistical evidence for improved free-energy estimation is weak. For Trp-cage and BBA, one of four runs is removed based on its final free-energy deviation from the mean, potentially suppressing precisely the trapping failures that the benchmark should measure. Remaining uncertainties are large, and BIOEMU-CV still has a BBA free-energy error of 7.22 kJ/mol. Full-run results, uncertainty on paired differences, and stronger convergence diagnostics are needed.

The claim that time-lagged conditioning identifies slow dynamical information is only partially supported. There is no lag-time sensitivity study or direct validation of the conditional propagator. Table 13 gives mixed evidence: removing time lag improves Chignolin PMF MAE from 3.07 to 1.41, despite the text claiming improvement across both downstream tasks. Committor correlation and VAMP scores also do not consistently favor BIOEMU-CV.

The steering evaluation demonstrates target reaching, but does not establish physically representative transition-path sampling. Rapid biased trajectories and maximum absolute potential energy, averaged only over successful paths, are insufficient to validate transition-state quality or path probabilities. Moreover, steering uses CHARMM36 at 340 K, whereas the reference landscapes use different simulation conditions, limiting interpretation of their projected agreement.

Reproducibility and scope remain limited. The training lag in physical units, time-pair construction after frame subsampling, optimizer settings, and conditioning-adapter specification are insufficiently documented. The protein experiments cover only three small systems, without establishing generalization beyond possible BioEmu pretraining overlap or isolating the benefit of pretraining against a matched generative model trained from scratch. These unresolved evaluation and attribution issues outweigh the promising empirical results at a top-tier acceptance threshold.
